title: Learning to aggregate Bayesian forecasts: optimal sample complexity under bounded dependence
shortTitle: How many resolved cases does forecast aggregation need?
oneLine: The exact rate, up to constants, for every level of dependence between experts: log(1/δ)/ε resolved cases when they are conditionally independent, (mⁿ + log(1/δ))/ε when anything goes.
abstract: Several forecasters each report a probability for the same yes/no event, each from different evidence. The best combination is the probability of the event given all the reports together, but it depends on how the forecasters' evidence overlaps, so an aggregator must learn it from a track record of past cases with known outcomes. In the binary model of Lin and Chen (NeurIPS 2023), with n experts whose evidence takes at most m values and exact, calibrated reports, earlier bounds differed by a factor 1/ε, and Lin and Chen conjectured that 1/ε is the right dependence on the accuracy. This candidate determines the answer up to universal constants for every level of dependence. With η a bound on the conditional total correlation of the reports given the outcome, T past cases and failure probability δ ≤ 1/32, the minimax excess Brier risk is of order min{1, log(1/δ)/T + min(η, mⁿ/T)}, and one estimator attains it without knowing η: it fits the multiplicative pooling formula and a lookup table and keeps whichever does better on held-out cases. So log(1/δ)/ε cases suffice and are needed under conditional independence, and (mⁿ + log(1/δ))/ε under arbitrary dependence, which raises Lin and Chen's mⁿ⁻² lower bound to mⁿ. For the independent case, standard localisation arguments already gave the upper bound up to a log T factor; the new parts there are removing that factor and the matching lower bounds. The hard examples keep every expert's calibration curve, the prior and the whole distribution of report vectors fixed. Further results cover a known prior, unbounded report alphabets and finitely many outcomes. Limits: exact, honest, calibrated reports; worst-case bounds with unoptimised constants; a factor of about k open for k outcomes. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem 1 (proof): for n, m ≥ 2, T ≥ 1, 0 < δ ≤ 1/32 and every dependence bound η, the minimax excess Brier risk lies between 2⁻¹⁷ and C times min{1, log(1/δ)/T + min(η, mⁿ/T)}, C universal; a single learning rule attains the upper bound for every η, m and δ.

Corollary 2 (proof): about log(1/δ)/ε cases are needed and suffice under conditional independence, and about (mⁿ + log(1/δ))/ε under arbitrary dependence; this confirms Lin and Chen's 1/ε conjecture for the binary model and raises their mⁿ⁻² lower bound to mⁿ.

Lemmas 4–6 and Section 3.4 (proof): assuming conditional independence costs at most half the conditional total correlation; least squares over the pointwise-ordered pooling family has no log T factor; validation chooses between the pooling and lookup-table candidates without knowing η.

Section 4 (proof, finite algebra checked exactly): the lower-bound alternatives share the prior, every expert's calibration curve and the whole law of the report vector, so no single expert's record and no unlabelled data can tell them apart; in the smallest case (m = n = 2) the reports are 31/64 and 33/64.

Propositions 7 and 8 (proof): with the prior known, no cases are needed when η ≤ 2ε; with unbounded report alphabets the rate is min{1, η + log(1/δ)/T}, so any fixed dependence allowance rules out uniform consistency.
Section 6 (proof): for k outcomes the dependence interpolation extends with constants depending on k; under conditional independence a factor of about k remains between the upper and lower bounds.

narration:
Suppose several forecasters each give a probability for the same yes or no question: will it rain tomorrow, will a patient relapse, who will win an election. Each has seen different evidence, and each reports honestly. The best way to combine them is the probability of the event given all their reports together. But that depends on how their evidence overlaps, and nobody knows that in advance. So an aggregator has to learn it from a track record of past cases whose outcomes are known. The question is how long that track record must be.

Earlier work set up this problem, found upper and lower answers that were far apart, and conjectured where the truth lay. This release settles the question, up to constant factors, for every level of overlap between the forecasters. If their evidence is independent once the outcome is known, the record needed grows only with the accuracy you want and the confidence you demand, not with the number of forecasters. If anything goes, it grows with the number of possible patterns of reports, which explodes as forecasters are added. In between, the answer moves smoothly with a measure of how much the forecasters share.

The practical message is simple. With a short record, use the classical pooling formula that multiplies the forecasters' odds, and accept a small bias from their shared evidence. Once the record is long enough, a lookup table over the patterns of reports can learn the shared structure. One method does both without knowing the overlap in advance: fit both, and keep whichever predicts better on cases held back for testing.

The hardest examples are striking. Every forecaster's own track record, the base rate, and even the full pattern of reports look identical, yet the right way to combine them differs. No single forecaster's history can reveal the difference.

Two honest caveats. For independent forecasters, standard tools from learning theory already gave almost the same answer; the new part there is removing an extra logarithmic factor and proving matching lower bounds. And the results assume exact, honest, calibrated forecasts, describe the worst case, and leave a gap when there are many possible outcomes. This is an unrefereed candidate, checked by internal AI-assisted review.

relatedWorks.citation: Agrawal (2020), Finite-sample concentration of the multinomial in relative entropy. IEEE Transactions on Information Theory. The concentration inequality behind the lookup-table bound.

Babichenko and Garber (2021), Learning optimal forecast aggregation in partial evidence environments. Mathematics of Operations Research. A related model of overlapping evidence; its sample complexity is posed as open.

Baraud and Chen (2024), Robust estimation of a regression function in exponential families. Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference. General robust bounds that give nearly inverse-linear rates with a logarithmic factor.
Bartlett, Bousquet and Mendelson (2005), Local Rademacher complexities. The Annals of Statistics. Localisation, which already gives the independent-case upper bound up to a log T factor.
Bordley (1982), A multiplicative formula for aggregating probability assessments. Management Science. The pooling formula, credited as in Lin and Chen (their Lemma 5.1).
Bousquet (2002), A Bennett concentration inequality and its application to suprema of empirical processes. Comptes Rendus Mathématique. The inequality used in the log-free least-squares lemma.
Koltchinskii (2006), Local Rademacher complexities and oracle inequalities in risk minimization. The Annals of Statistics. Localisation theory compared in Section 1.

Lin and Chen (2023), Sample complexity of forecast aggregation. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36. The model, the earlier bounds, the confidence lower bound and the 1/ε conjecture answered here.

decisionObject.description: Decide how many resolved past cases an aggregator needs to learn to combine calibrated probability forecasts, at each level of dependence between the forecasters, and when a simple pooling formula should be preferred to learning the joint structure.
decisionObject.scope: Binary outcomes; n experts with at most m signal values each; exact calibrated reports; independent training cases; worst case over all laws with a given dependence bound; extensions to unbounded alphabets and finitely many outcomes.
